title: The paradox of choice
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (multiple choice, extended text)
text:
Walk into any large supermarket and you will be confronted with an astonishing array of options: dozens of breakfast cereals, hundreds of varieties of yoghurt, entire aisles devoted to shampoo. For most of human history, such abundance would have been unimaginable, and it is tempting to assume that it has made us happier. After all, more choice means a greater chance of finding exactly what we want. Yet a substantial body of research suggests that, beyond a certain point, the opposite may be true.
The phenomenon was popularised by the psychologist Barry Schwartz, who coined the phrase 'the paradox of choice'. Schwartz argued that an excess of options can lead not to satisfaction but to anxiety, paralysis and regret. His argument drew on a now-famous experiment conducted in a California grocery store. On one day, shoppers were offered samples from a display of twenty-four different jams; on another, the display contained just six. The larger display attracted more attention, but when it came to actually buying, the results were striking: shoppers who had seen the smaller selection were roughly ten times more likely to make a purchase.
Why should this be? One explanation is that evaluating options takes mental effort. When faced with a handful of alternatives, we can compare them with relative ease. Confronted with dozens, we become overwhelmed, and the simplest response is often to walk away without deciding at all. Even when we do choose, an abundance of options raises our expectations. If there are fifty kinds of jeans available, surely one of them must be perfect, and any pair that falls short feels like a failure, one for which we hold ourselves responsible.
Schwartz also distinguished between two types of decision-makers. 'Maximisers' feel compelled to examine every possibility in order to find the best one, while 'satisficers' are content to settle for something that meets their criteria, even if something better might exist. Counter-intuitively, studies suggest that maximisers often end up with objectively better outcomes, such as higher-paying jobs, yet report feeling less satisfied with them. Their constant awareness of the alternatives they rejected seems to rob them of the pleasure of what they have chosen.
It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that choice is inherently harmful. Later attempts to replicate the jam experiment produced mixed results, and a large analysis of similar studies found that the effect of choice overload varies considerably depending on the circumstances. When people already know what they want, or when options are clearly organised, a wide selection poses few problems. Difficulties arise mainly when the choices are complex, hard to compare, and made under time pressure.
Nor should we overlook the fact that the freedom to choose is something many people around the world still lack. The ability to decide where to live, what to study or whom to marry is hardly a burden to be lamented. The problem, if there is one, lies less in choice itself than in the belief that every decision must be optimal.
What practical lessons can be drawn? Some psychologists recommend deliberately limiting the options we consider, setting clear criteria in advance, and accepting 'good enough' for decisions that do not really matter. Others suggest cultivating gratitude for what we have chosen rather than dwelling on what we gave up. These strategies will not eliminate the dilemmas of modern life, but they may make the cereal aisle feel a little less daunting.

options: It has been completely disproved by later research

title: The forgotten pandemic
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
Between 1918 and 1920, an influenza pandemic swept across the globe, infecting roughly a third of the world's population and killing somewhere between twenty and fifty million people, possibly more. It claimed more lives than the First World War, which was drawing to a close as the virus spread. And yet, for much of the twentieth century, this catastrophe occupied a remarkably small place in public memory. There were few monuments, few novels, few films. Historians have long puzzled over why an event of such magnitude was so quickly forgotten.
Part of the explanation lies in its timing. The pandemic arrived at a moment when people had already endured four years of unprecedented slaughter. War had a clear narrative, with heroes, villains, battles and, eventually, a victory to commemorate. Disease offered none of these. People did not die fighting for a cause; they died in their beds, often within days of feeling the first symptoms. There was nothing to celebrate and no one to blame, and grief of this kind does not lend itself easily to public ceremony.
Censorship also played a role. Fearing damage to morale, the governments of countries involved in the war suppressed reports of the outbreak. Spain, which was neutral and had a relatively free press, reported openly on the disease, with the unfortunate consequence that it became known around the world as the 'Spanish flu', even though there is no evidence it originated there. Modern researchers have proposed several possible origins, including military camps in the United States and France, but the question remains unresolved.
The medical response was hampered by ignorance. Viruses had not yet been identified, and many doctors believed influenza was caused by a bacterium. There were no vaccines, no antiviral drugs and no antibiotics to treat the secondary infections that killed many patients. Authorities fell back on measures that would be familiar today: closing schools, theatres and churches, banning public gatherings and encouraging, or in some cases requiring, the wearing of masks. Cities that acted early and decisively tended to suffer lower death rates, although such measures were frequently resisted by those who regarded them as unnecessary or an infringement of their liberty.
One of the most unsettling features of the 1918 pandemic was the age of its victims. Influenza normally poses the greatest danger to the very young and the very old. This time, an unusually high proportion of deaths occurred among healthy adults between twenty and forty. Scientists still debate why; one theory suggests that older people had gained some immunity from an earlier, similar strain, while another proposes that the immune systems of young adults overreacted to the virus, causing fatal damage to their own lungs.
Interest in the pandemic revived towards the end of the century, as scientists recovered samples of the virus from victims buried in the Alaskan permafrost and reconstructed its genetic code. It intensified dramatically after 2020, when the world was confronted with a new pandemic and found, perhaps uncomfortably, that many of the debates of 1918 were being repeated almost word for word.
The story of the 'forgotten pandemic' is therefore not merely a historical curiosity. It is a reminder that societies tend to remember what fits a comforting narrative, and to forget what does not, and that forgetting carries its own risks.

options: Why the 1918 pandemic began in Spain
Why a deadly pandemic was largely forgotten and what it can teach us
The military history of the First World War

options: Spain had the highest death rate

questions.prompt: In the text, 'hampered' is closest in meaning to:
Complete: Unusually, many victims were healthy adults between twenty and ___.

options: Collective forgetting can leave societies unprepared
The 1918 pandemic was less serious than claimed

Modern debates about pandemics are entirely new

title: Who is responsible when algorithms decide?
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (opinion piece)
text:
Not long ago, the idea that a computer program might decide whether you get a job interview, a mortgage or parole would have sounded like the plot of a dystopian novel. Today it is routine. Algorithms sift through CVs, assess credit risk, predict which neighbourhoods are likely to see crime and recommend which patients should receive additional medical care. Their defenders argue, with some justification, that they are faster, cheaper and more consistent than human beings. Yet as automated decision-making spreads, a troubling question has emerged: when an algorithm gets it wrong, who is to blame?
The question is less straightforward than it might appear. Modern systems based on machine learning are not programmed with explicit rules in the traditional sense. Instead, they are trained on vast quantities of historical data and learn to identify patterns. The difficulty is that historical data often reflects historical injustice. A widely reported case involved a large technology company that developed a tool to rank job applicants. Because it had been trained on the CVs of people hired over the previous decade, most of whom were men, the system learned to penalise applications that mentioned women's organisations or all-female colleges. Nobody had instructed it to discriminate; it had simply absorbed the biases of the past.
Compounding the problem is the issue of transparency. Many algorithms are so complex that even their designers struggle to explain why a particular decision was reached. Others are protected as commercial secrets, meaning that the people affected by them have no way of examining how they work. A person refused a loan by a human bank manager can at least ask for an explanation; one refused by an opaque system may receive nothing more than a standard letter.
It is tempting to respond by banning such systems altogether, but that would be naive. Human decision-makers are hardly free of prejudice; numerous studies have shown that judges, doctors and recruiters can be influenced by factors as irrelevant as a candidate's name or the time of day. A well-designed algorithm, carefully tested for bias, could in principle be fairer than the people it replaces. The real issue is not whether we use algorithms, but how we govern them.
Several principles are beginning to gain acceptance. First, organisations that deploy automated systems should remain accountable for their outcomes; 'the computer decided' must never be an acceptable defence. Second, people should have the right to know when a significant decision about them has been made by a machine, and to have it reviewed by a human being. Third, systems used in sensitive areas such as employment, healthcare and criminal justice should be independently audited, both before and after they are introduced, to detect discriminatory effects.
The stakes are particularly high in criminal justice. In some jurisdictions, risk-assessment tools have been used to inform decisions about bail and sentencing, estimating how likely a defendant is to reoffend. Investigations have suggested that certain tools wrongly labelled defendants from minority groups as high-risk far more often than others, raising serious doubts about whether such systems should play any role in decisions about a person's liberty.
None of this will be simple. Regulation risks lagging years behind the technology, and companies will inevitably argue that excessive oversight stifles innovation. But the alternative, allowing decisions that shape people's lives to be made by systems nobody fully understands or controls, is far worse. Technology may change how decisions are made. It should not change who answers for them.

options: Algorithms should be banned in sensitive areas
Algorithms are always fairer than humans
The use of algorithms needs clear accountability and oversight
Companies should keep their algorithms secret

options: It learned from biased historical data

options: impossible to understand or see into

What does the final sentence suggest?
options: Decisions should be made more quickly

title: The death of languages
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
Somewhere in the world, roughly every few months, a language dies. It rarely makes the news. Often the moment passes unnoticed: an elderly speaker, the last person who learned the language as a child, quietly passes away, and with them goes a way of describing the world that took thousands of years to develop. Of the approximately seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that around forty per cent are endangered, and some predict that by the end of the century half of them could have disappeared.
Languages have always come and gone, of course. Latin gave way to Italian, Spanish and French; countless languages of the ancient world vanished without leaving a trace. What is different today is the speed and scale of the loss. Globalisation, urbanisation and the dominance of a small number of major languages in education, business and the media have created powerful incentives for parents to raise their children in whichever language seems to offer the best economic prospects. In many cases, communities have also faced deliberate suppression: until surprisingly recently, children in several countries were punished for speaking their indigenous language at school.
Why should this matter to anyone who does not speak one of these languages? One argument is scientific. Each language encodes a particular way of perceiving and organising experience. Some languages have no words for 'left' and 'right', describing positions instead in terms of compass directions, so that a speaker might mention the ant 'on your north-east leg'. Others distinguish grammatically between events the speaker witnessed personally and those they only heard about. Such features offer valuable insights into the range of human cognition, insights that are lost forever when a language dies undocumented.
There is also a practical dimension. Indigenous languages frequently contain detailed knowledge about local plants, animals and ecosystems, accumulated over generations. Researchers have found that when communities shift to a dominant language, much of this knowledge, including information about medicinal plants, fails to make the transition.
Yet perhaps the most compelling argument concerns identity. For many communities, language is inseparable from history, ritual and a sense of belonging. Losing it can feel like losing a part of oneself, and studies in several countries have linked the revival of indigenous languages to improvements in young people's wellbeing.
The good news is that decline is not inevitable. The most celebrated example of revival is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious texts and was transformed into the everyday language of millions. More modest successes include Welsh, whose number of speakers has stabilised thanks to bilingual education and broadcasting, and Māori in New Zealand, where 'language nests' immerse young children in the language from an early age. Technology, which is often blamed for accelerating language loss, is also playing a part, through recordings, online dictionaries and apps that allow scattered speakers to stay in contact.
Revival requires sustained effort and, crucially, the commitment of the community itself; no outside organisation can save a language that its potential speakers do not wish to use. But the examples above show that, with enough determination, a language that seemed destined for silence can find its voice again.

title: The myth of multitasking
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In job advertisements, the ability to multitask is frequently listed as a desirable quality, as if juggling several activities at once were a skill to be proud of. Many of us believe we are rather good at it. We answer emails during meetings, check our phones while helping children with their homework and listen to podcasts while writing reports. Yet according to a growing body of neuroscientific research, true multitasking is largely an illusion, and our attempts at it come at a considerable cost.
The human brain, it turns out, cannot genuinely concentrate on two cognitively demanding tasks simultaneously. What we experience as multitasking is in fact rapid task-switching: the brain shifts its attention back and forth, sometimes several times a second. Each switch carries what psychologists call a 'switch cost', a brief delay while the brain disengages from one set of rules and reorients itself to another. Individually these delays are tiny, but they accumulate. Some estimates suggest that habitual switching can reduce productivity by as much as forty per cent.
The effects are not limited to speed. Studies have found that people who frequently switch between tasks make more errors and remember less of what they have done. In one experiment, participants who were interrupted while reading a text scored significantly lower on a comprehension test than those who read without interruption, even when they were given extra time to compensate. Perhaps most strikingly, research comparing heavy and light media multitaskers found that the heavy multitaskers performed worse at filtering out irrelevant information, the very skill one might expect them to have developed through practice.
There are exceptions. When one activity is so familiar that it has become automatic, such as walking or folding laundry, we can combine it with another task without much difficulty. This is why most people can listen to music while running. Problems arise when both tasks require conscious thought, or when the stakes are high. Using a phone while driving is the most dangerous example: even hands-free conversations have been shown to slow reaction times to a degree comparable with driving over the legal alcohol limit.
Why, then, do we persist? Part of the answer is that multitasking feels productive. Switching between activities provides a constant stream of novelty, which the brain finds rewarding, and the sensation of being busy is easily mistaken for achievement. Modern technology, with its endless notifications, actively encourages fragmented attention, and many workplaces implicitly expect employees to respond instantly to every message.
Some organisations are beginning to push back. Companies have experimented with email-free afternoons, meeting-free days and policies discouraging out-of-hours messaging. Individuals can adopt similar strategies: turning off notifications, grouping similar tasks together and setting aside uninterrupted blocks of time for demanding work. The writer Cal Newport has popularised the term 'deep work' to describe this kind of sustained concentration, arguing that it is becoming both increasingly rare and increasingly valuable.
The consequences extend to education as well. Teachers report that students who keep their phones on their desks during homework take considerably longer to finish and retain less of what they have studied. Even the mere presence of a phone, switched off and face down, has been found in some studies to reduce performance on demanding tasks, presumably because part of the mind remains alert to it.
None of this means we must return to a world without smartphones. But it does suggest that, when it comes to work that truly matters, doing one thing at a time may be not old-fashioned but essential.

options: Multitasking is a valuable skill for modern workers

options: They were better at ignoring irrelevant information

title: The rewilding debate
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In 1995, after an absence of nearly seventy years, grey wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in the United States. What happened next has become one of the most famous stories in modern ecology. With wolves once again hunting them, elk changed their behaviour, avoiding open valleys where they were vulnerable. Freed from constant grazing, willow and aspen trees began to recover along riverbanks. Their roots stabilised the soil, beavers returned to use the trees, and the dams they built created new habitats for fish, birds and amphibians. The return of a single predator, it seemed, had set off a cascade of changes that transformed the landscape.
The Yellowstone story has become a rallying cry for 'rewilding', a conservation approach that aims to restore natural processes rather than manage nature in minute detail. Instead of protecting a particular species in a small reserve, rewilders seek to reconnect fragmented habitats, reintroduce missing animals and then, as far as possible, step back and let nature take its course. Projects inspired by this philosophy have spread across the world, from the return of bison to parts of Romania to the release of beavers in the British countryside.
Yet the approach is not without its critics, and the debate has become increasingly heated. Some scientists argue that the Yellowstone narrative has been oversimplified. More recent research suggests that the recovery of trees was patchy and that factors such as hunting by humans, drought and the activities of bears also played important roles. Ecosystems, they caution, rarely respond to a single change in such a neat and predictable way.
The fiercest opposition, however, tends to come from those who live and work in the areas concerned. For farmers, the return of predators can mean the loss of livestock and, with it, income. In parts of Europe where wolf populations have grown in recent decades, conflicts have intensified, with some governments under pressure to relax legal protections. Critics also argue that rewilding is often promoted by wealthy urban conservationists who do not have to live with the consequences, and that it risks turning working landscapes, which have been shaped by human hands for centuries, into wilderness designed for visitors.
Supporters respond that many of these concerns can be addressed. Compensation schemes can reimburse farmers for animals killed by predators, while guard dogs and electric fencing have proved effective at reducing attacks. Rewilding projects can also generate new sources of income through eco-tourism, and some of the most successful have been led by local communities rather than imposed from outside. They point out, too, that the alternative, continuing with business as usual, is hardly risk-free, given the alarming rate at which biodiversity is declining.
Rewilding also raises questions about which version of nature we are trying to restore. Landscapes have changed continuously over thousands of years, and there is no obvious 'original' state to return to. Some ecologists therefore prefer to focus on restoring functions, such as natural flooding or grazing, rather than attempting to recreate a particular moment in the past, which may no longer suit today's changing climate.
Perhaps the most productive way forward is to recognise that rewilding is not a single blueprint but a spectrum. At one end lie ambitious projects involving large predators; at the other, modest initiatives such as allowing a corner of a farm to grow wild or restoring a stretch of river to its natural course. The question is not simply whether to rewild, but how, where and with whom.

title: Exams: measuring what matters?
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (opinion piece)
text:
Every summer, in countries all over the world, millions of teenagers sit in silent halls, turning over exam papers that will, they are told, shape the rest of their lives. For a few weeks, the whole education system seems to revolve around these moments. Teachers adapt their lessons to the demands of the syllabus, parents pay for private tutoring, and newspapers publish tables ranking schools according to their results. It is worth asking, though, whether this enormous effort is measuring the things that really matter.
The case for traditional exams is not to be dismissed lightly. They are, at least in principle, fair: every candidate answers the same questions under the same conditions, and the marking is anonymous. Unlike coursework, which can be completed with the help of parents or, increasingly, artificial intelligence, an exam provides reasonable assurance that the work is the student's own. Exams also motivate many students to review material they would otherwise neglect, and research on memory suggests that the act of retrieving information, as one does when revising, strengthens learning.
The problems arise when exams become not one tool among many but the overriding purpose of schooling. When schools are judged by their results, there is an inevitable temptation to 'teach to the test', concentrating on the predictable question types and exam techniques at the expense of deeper understanding. Subjects and skills that are hard to assess in a timed written paper, such as collaboration, creativity, practical problem-solving and oral communication, tend to be squeezed out. Ironically, these are precisely the abilities that employers say they value most.
There is also the question of what exams actually reward. A three-hour paper tests a particular combination of knowledge, memory, speed and the ability to perform under pressure. Some students thrive in such conditions; others, including many who are capable and hard-working, do not. Anxiety, illness or a family crisis in the week of the exam can have a disproportionate effect on a result that may determine access to university. A single grade inevitably conceals as much as it reveals.
Several countries have experimented with alternatives. Finland, often praised for its education system, has no national standardised exams until the end of secondary school, relying instead on teachers' continuous assessment. Other systems combine exams with portfolios of work, extended research projects or oral presentations. Each approach has its drawbacks; continuous assessment, for instance, can place heavy demands on teachers and is more vulnerable to inconsistency. But a mixture of methods is likely to produce a more rounded picture of a student's abilities than any single test.
The pressure on students themselves should not be underestimated either. Surveys in several countries have recorded rising levels of exam-related stress among teenagers, with significant numbers reporting sleeplessness, panic attacks and a sense that their future depends entirely on a handful of days. For some, the experience leaves a lasting association between learning and anxiety that can discourage them from further study long after they have left school. Teachers, meanwhile, describe feeling trapped between their own educational ideals and the relentless pressure to deliver results.
The goal, surely, should not be to abolish exams but to put them in their proper place: as a useful snapshot of certain kinds of achievement, rather than the final verdict on a young person's worth. An education system that produces excellent test-takers but anxious, uninspired learners has confused the measurement with the thing being measured.

options: Exams are the fairest possible system and should not change

title: Why do we sleep?
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (popular science)
text:
We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep, lying unconscious and vulnerable for hours at a time. From an evolutionary perspective, this is puzzling. An animal that is asleep cannot search for food, look after its young or escape from predators. If sleep did not serve some vital purpose, natural selection would surely have eliminated it long ago. Yet virtually every animal studied, from fruit flies to whales, sleeps in some form. Dolphins even sleep with one half of their brain at a time, so that they can continue to swim and surface to breathe.
For most of history, the purpose of sleep was a mystery, and even today scientists do not agree on a single answer. What has become clear, however, is that sleep is far from a passive state. During the night, the brain cycles through distinct stages, each associated with characteristic patterns of electrical activity, and each appears to perform different functions.
One of the most important of these concerns memory. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay experiences from the day, transferring information from the hippocampus, a region involved in forming new memories, to the cortex, where it can be stored for the long term. In experiments, people who sleep after learning a list of words or a new motor skill consistently perform better when tested the following day than those who stay awake for the same period. Sleep also seems to help us extract general rules from specific experiences; in one study, participants were more than twice as likely to discover a hidden shortcut in a mathematical problem after a night's sleep.
Another function, discovered relatively recently, is cleaning. During waking hours, the brain's activity produces waste products, including proteins associated with Alzheimer's disease. Research on mice has suggested that during sleep, the spaces between brain cells expand, allowing fluid to flow through and wash away these substances more efficiently. If this finding is confirmed in humans, it may help to explain why chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
The consequences of insufficient sleep extend far beyond the brain. Even a few nights of reduced sleep can disrupt the hormones that regulate appetite, leading people to feel hungrier and to crave sugary foods. Long-term sleep deprivation has been associated with obesity, diabetes, heart disease and a weakened immune system. Tired people are also more irritable, less able to regulate their emotions and more likely to have accidents.
Despite this evidence, sleep is often treated as a luxury, or even as a sign of weakness. Many people boast about how little they sleep, and long working hours, late-night screen use and the culture of constant connectivity have all contributed to what some researchers describe as a global sleep crisis.
Dreams, which occur mainly during the stage known as REM sleep, remain more mysterious. Some researchers believe they help us process emotional experiences, softening the impact of painful memories; others suspect they are simply a by-product of the brain's night-time activity. Interestingly, people who are woken repeatedly during REM sleep often report feeling more anxious and emotionally fragile the following day.
The advice from scientists is consistent: most adults need between seven and nine hours a night, and regular timing matters almost as much as duration. Sleep, it turns out, is not time taken away from a productive life. It is one of the foundations on which such a life is built.

options: To describe research into the functions and importance of sleep

options: Waste products are washed away more efficiently

options: To suggest sleep must have an important purpose

title: The fifteen-minute city
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
Imagine being able to reach your workplace, your children's school, a doctor, a park, a supermarket and a café within a fifteen-minute walk or bike ride from your front door. For residents of many suburbs, where even buying a pint of milk requires a car journey, this might sound like a fantasy. For the urban planners who champion the 'fifteen-minute city', it is a realistic and urgently needed goal.
The concept was popularised by Carlos Moreno, a professor at the Sorbonne in Paris, and was enthusiastically adopted by the city's mayor, Anne Hidalgo, as part of her re-election campaign in 2020. Its central idea is simple: instead of organising cities around long commutes between separate zones for living, working and shopping, planners should create neighbourhoods where most daily needs can be met locally. In practice, this means encouraging a mixture of housing, shops, offices and services in every district, redesigning streets to favour pedestrians and cyclists, and making better use of existing buildings; school playgrounds, for example, can be opened to the public at weekends.
The potential benefits are considerable. Fewer car journeys mean less traffic, cleaner air and lower carbon emissions. Time saved on commuting can be spent with family or friends. Supporters argue that the approach also strengthens communities, since people who walk around their neighbourhood are more likely to meet their neighbours and support local businesses. The disruption caused by the pandemic, when many people found themselves working from home and rediscovering their local area, added to the idea's appeal.
In recent years, however, the fifteen-minute city has become the subject of an unexpectedly fierce controversy. In several countries, opponents have claimed that it is a plot to restrict people's freedom of movement, confining them to their own districts and fining them for leaving. These claims, which spread rapidly on social media, misrepresent the concept, which is about adding local amenities rather than imposing restrictions. Nevertheless, some of the anger reflects genuine concerns. Measures that sometimes accompany such schemes, such as closing roads to through traffic, can lengthen journeys for those who depend on cars, including tradespeople, carers and disabled people. Residents of poorer areas also worry that improvements to their neighbourhoods will attract wealthier newcomers, pushing up rents.
There are practical limitations too. The model works most naturally in dense, older European cities, where shops and services are already relatively close together. It is far harder to apply in sprawling suburbs designed around the car, where creating local services from scratch requires major investment and changes to planning laws. Critics also point out that no neighbourhood can provide everything; specialist hospitals, universities and many jobs will always be concentrated in particular places.
Paris has already made visible changes. Hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes have been created, some streets near schools have been closed to cars and turned into green spaces, and the riverside roads along the Seine have been converted into areas for walking and leisure. Cities such as Barcelona, Melbourne and Bogotá have introduced similar policies, adapting the idea to their own geography and needs.
Moreno himself has acknowledged that the fifteen-minute figure is less a strict rule than a way of starting a conversation about how cities should work. The ultimate aim, he argues, is to give people more choice, not less: the possibility of living well without being forced to spend hours every day in a car or on a crowded train.

title: Can machines be creative?
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In 2018, a portrait of a blurred, vaguely aristocratic gentleman sold at a major auction house for over four hundred thousand dollars. Nothing about the painting itself was especially remarkable. What made it newsworthy was its creator: the image had been produced not by a human artist but by an algorithm, trained on thousands of portraits painted between the fourteenth and twentieth centuries. Since then, the capabilities of such systems have advanced at a startling pace. Programs can now generate photorealistic images, compose music in the style of any composer and write poems on any subject in a matter of seconds. The question that philosophers once debated in the abstract has become urgently practical: can a machine be creative?
The answer depends, of course, on what we mean by creativity. One widely used definition holds that a creative product must be both novel and valuable: it must be new, and it must be useful, beautiful or meaningful in some way. By this standard, it is difficult to deny that machines can produce creative outputs. Their images and texts are frequently original in the sense that no identical work has existed before, and many people find them genuinely appealing.
Sceptics, however, argue that this definition misses something essential. Current systems, they point out, work by identifying statistical patterns in enormous quantities of existing human work and recombining them. They have no intentions, no experiences and nothing they are trying to express. A machine that writes a poem about grief has never lost anyone. For these critics, creativity is not merely a property of the finished product but of the process that produces it, and that process involves a conscious mind with something to say.
Defenders of machine creativity respond that human artists, too, learn by absorbing and recombining the work of others. No painter emerges from nowhere; every writer is shaped by what they have read. If novelty arising from recombination is acceptable when humans do it, why not when machines do? Moreover, they note, we often value works of art without knowing anything about the intentions of their creators.
Beyond the philosophical debate lie pressing practical concerns. Many artists, illustrators and writers object that their work has been used to train commercial systems without their permission or any payment, and several have taken legal action. Others fear for their livelihoods, as businesses discover that they can generate images or texts more cheaply than they can commission them. At the same time, some artists have embraced the technology as a tool, using it to explore ideas, generate rough drafts or create works that would otherwise be impossible, much as photography and digital editing were once regarded with suspicion before becoming accepted artistic media.
The legal status of machine-generated work is equally unsettled. In several countries, copyright law protects only works created by human authors, which means that an image produced entirely by an algorithm may belong to no one at all. Courts and governments are now struggling to decide where the line should be drawn when a human and a machine collaborate, and how much human input is enough.
Perhaps the most likely outcome is not that machines will replace human creativity, but that they will change its nature and its value. When polished images and competent prose become cheap and abundant, what may become scarce, and therefore precious, is the distinctly human element: a personal perspective, a lived experience, a voice that could only belong to one particular person.
